title: What pattern hides in three numbers in a row?
description: Three numbers in a row are chosen, the middle one is squared, and the multiplication of the other two is taken away. Examples show a pattern, and letters prove it for every set.
teaching_notes: One idea: call the three numbers n minus one, n and n plus one, multiply out, and see the result is always one. Watch for students who stop after the examples and call the pattern proved.

source: Figure it Out (identities and patterns, question 7)
video_script.why: The child can multiply out two brackets, but has not yet used letters to explain a pattern seen in sets of numbers.
video_script.substitution: Call the middle number n, write its neighbours with n, and multiply out the way the cards in the book did.
video_script.anchor: three numbers in a row from the book's question, with the middle one squared
video_script.payoff_line: The answer is always one, for every set of three numbers in a row.

final_answer.spoken: the answer is always one, for every set of three numbers in a row

maths_rules: the numbers are n − 1, n and n + 1
video_script.design: One idea: examples show the pattern and letters prove it. The three numbers stay on the board through the idea part. The take away that gives one is left until the answer.

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book.
<bookmark mark='row'/>Choose three numbers in a row, like five, six and seven.
<bookmark mark='mid'/>Square the middle one.
<bookmark mark='ends'/>Then take away what you get by multiplying the other two.

beats.on_screen: the three tiles stay on the board; Keeko sits at the corner of the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: the three tiles relabelled n - 1, n, n + 1, with arrows: one step left from n is -1, one step right is +1

marks.arrows: an arrow one step left of the middle tile is marked -1, and an arrow one step right is marked +1
marks.letters: the three tiles are relabelled n - 1, n and n + 1

beats.colours: the -1 arrow and the +1 arrow in two colours
narration: <bookmark mark='arrows'/>The number before the middle one is one less. The number after it is one more.
<bookmark mark='letters'/>Call the middle number n. The three numbers are n minus one, n, and n plus one.

beats.on_screen: Given: three numbers in a row, n - 1, n, n + 1
narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, three numbers in a row.

beats.on_screen: To find: the pattern, and why it holds

marks.find: the words to find are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the pattern, and why it holds.
<bookmark mark='five'/>Step one, try some sets. For five, six and seven, thirty six minus thirty five leaves one.
<bookmark mark='nine'/>For nine, ten and eleven, one hundred minus ninety nine leaves one.

marks.write: n² - (n - 1)(n + 1) is written as the same steps with letters

narration: <bookmark mark='write'/>Step two, write the same steps with letters. The middle squared is n squared. We take away n minus one times n plus one.

marks.parts: n x n = n², n x 1 = n, -1 x n = -n and -1 x 1 = -1 are written as the four parts
marks.more: the parts n and -n are written next to each other
marks.sum: n - n = 0 is written, giving n² - 1

beats.colours: the like terms in one colour
narration: <bookmark mark='parts'/>Step three, multiply out the brackets. N times n is n squared, and n times one is n.
<bookmark mark='more'/>Minus one times n is minus n, and minus one times one is minus one.
<bookmark mark='sum'/>Plus n and minus n cancel, so we are left with n squared minus one.

marks.put: n² - (n² - 1) is written, with the brackets around n² - 1

narration: <bookmark mark='put'/>Step four, put that in. We have n squared, take away n squared minus one.

marks.pick: n = 20 is chosen, and 19, 20, 21 are written

narration: <bookmark mark='pick'/>Step five, put the answer back in the question. Take n as twenty, so the numbers are nineteen, twenty and twenty one.
<bookmark mark='mult'/>Twenty squared is four hundred. Nineteen times twenty one is three hundred ninety nine.
<bookmark mark='tick'/>Four hundred minus three hundred ninety nine is one.
<bookmark mark='ans'/>The answer is always one, for every set of three numbers in a row.
<bookmark mark='why'/>Taking n squared minus one away from n squared leaves one, whatever n is.
